move: Holds the moral law to be an objective determining principle of good and evil whose motivating feeling of respect originates in pure practical reason rather than in any antecedent sensible inclination.

Insists the moral imperative's objective necessity cannot rest on any hypothesis, yet concedes no example can show empirically that a will was determined by the law alone, leaving open that all apparently categorical imperatives are at bottom hypothetical.
Answers the 'too demanding' objection by separating the rule of action from the motive, arguing that ethics supplies a test of duty while motive bears only on the worth of the agent.

Grounds morality in an objective principle of universal legislation binding on every rational being, with duty resting solely on rational beings' relation to one another and not on feelings, impulses, or inclinations.
Argues morals must first be treated as a pure metaphysic complete in itself, independent of anthropology, or they cannot be based on their genuine principles at all.
Contrasts market value and fancy value with the intrinsic worth of moral dispositions, whose dignity requires no recommendation from subjective taste or sentiment and is imposed by reason alone.
Declares intention-morality a prejudice of the same rank as astrology and alchemy, treating intention as a sign with too many interpretations and calling for morality to be surmounted.
Argues that even benevolent inclination and compassion cannot produce moral worth, since morality rather than mere legality requires the conception of the law itself as determining principle.

Notes that the intuitive and inductive schools alike affirm a science of morals deduced from principles, and faults them for failing to supply the self-evident first principle such a science requires.
Assigns moral feeling to pure reason alone and denies it any role in founding the objective moral law, which it serves only as a motive.

Defends utility as a workable test by appealing to mankind's accumulated experience of the effects of actions on happiness, while maintaining that the received code has no divine right and admits of indefinite improvement.
Discusses only the external sanctions that could attach to utilitarian morality, expressly bracketing whether there is any ground of moral obligation besides general happiness.
